solutions.text: Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Some people demonstrate remarkable resilience in the face of hardship, bouncing back far faster than others. — "Resilience" là danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được, thường đi với "remarkable/psychological resilience" hoặc "resilience in the face of adversity".

2. A good counsellor needs a high degree of empathy in order to understand what a client is feeling from the inside. — "Empathy" (đặt mình vào cảm xúc người khác), khác với "sympathy" (thương cảm); thường đi với "show/cultivate empathy towards sb".

3. Many patients say that finally talking about a painful memory is a cathartic experience, bringing an enormous emotional release. — "Cathartic" là tính từ, hay đi với "a cathartic experience/moment"; chú ý "th" phát âm /θ/, không phải /k/.

4. Scientists now agree that a child's brain remains malleable well into adulthood, capable of being shaped and changed. — "Malleable" (dễ uốn nắn về tư duy/tính cách), thường dùng với "remain malleable" hoặc "a malleable mind".

5. Some of our habits are governed by subconscious processes that we are not even aware of. — "Subconscious" (tiềm thức, vẫn ảnh hưởng hành vi dù ta không ý thức được), khác với "unconscious" (bất tỉnh); hay đi với "subconscious biases/the subconscious mind".

6. Volunteers who give up their weekends to help strangers without expecting anything in return demonstrate genuine altruism. — "Altruism" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ lòng vị tha; không dùng để miêu tả trực tiếp một người, nên đi với "an act of altruism" hoặc "genuine/pure altruism".
7. Constantly posting edited photos for admiration can be a sign of narcissism. — "Narcissism" là danh từ (chứng ái kỷ); tính từ tương ứng là "narcissistic", không phải "narcissism behaviour".

8. Keeping a journal for quiet introspection can reveal thought patterns you never noticed. — "Introspection" (tự xét nội tâm), khác với "inspection" (kiểm tra bên ngoài); hay đi với "a period of introspection" hoặc "practise introspection".

9. Because both of her parents suffered from anxiety, she may have a genetic predisposition to developing it too. — Cấu trúc chuẩn là "a predisposition to/towards sth", không dùng "for"; đây là khuynh hướng bẩm sinh, thường do di truyền.

10. Losing a parent at a young age can leave a lasting psychological trauma that lingers for decades. — "Trauma" (sang chấn tâm lý), khác với "stress" (căng thẳng nhẹ, tạm thời); hay đi với "childhood/psychological trauma" hoặc "process/overcome trauma".

11. The doctor explained that her chronic headaches were entirely psychosomatic, with no physical cause to be found. — "Psychosomatic" (triệu chứng thể chất bắt nguồn từ tâm lý); chữ "p" đầu là âm câm, trọng âm rơi vào "MAT".

12. Researchers are still grappling with why some people recover from depression faster than others. — "Grapple with" luôn đi kèm giới từ "with" (vật lộn để giải quyết một vấn đề khó), không dùng "grapple sth".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: Chronic stress can trigger psychosomatic symptoms even when there is no underlying physical illness. Band 8: What often goes unnoticed is that the body can manifest psychological strain as genuine physical symptoms — a phenomenon clinicians term psychosomatic illness. (cleft + nominalisation)

2. Band 7: Children who receive consistent parental affection tend to grow up with greater self-confidence and emotional security. Band 8: It is, in large part, the quality of early parental bonds — as attachment theory suggests — that shapes a child's confidence well into adulthood. (cleft + reduced relative)

3. Band 7: People often fall prey to confirmation bias, favouring information that supports their existing beliefs. Band 8: Rarely do we seek out evidence that contradicts our convictions; instead, confirmation bias quietly steers us towards whatever confirms what we already believe. (negative inversion)

4. Band 7: Regular physical exercise can significantly alleviate symptoms of anxiety and low mood. Band 8: Were exercise prescribed as readily as medication, the burden of anxiety and depressive symptoms would, in all likelihood, be considerably lighter. (conditional inversion + hedging)

5. Band 7: A difficult childhood can have a lasting psychological impact that persists well into adulthood. Band 8: Traumatic as a difficult childhood may be, its effects, in most cases, can be mitigated through sustained therapeutic intervention and a supportive environment. (concession inversion + hedging)

6. Band 7: Governments should allocate significantly more resources to mental health services and early intervention. Band 8: Not only would greater investment in mental health services ease individual suffering, but it would also, on virtually any reading of the evidence, yield substantial economic returns. (negative inversion + hedging)

7. Band 7: Therapy can help individuals gain insight into the underlying causes of their behaviour. Band 8: It is through sustained introspection, guided by a trained therapist, that individuals typically come to understand the root causes of their own behaviour. (cleft + reduced relative)

8. Band 7: Excessive exposure to social media can exacerbate young people's tendency to compare themselves unfavourably with others. Band 8: What social media exacerbates, more than anything else, is a corrosive culture of comparison — one that leaves many young people questioning their own self-worth. (cleft + nominalisation)

passages.text: For most of the twentieth century, replication occupied a curiously minor place in the practical economy of psychological research. A textbook would describe a celebrated experiment — the conformity studies of Solomon Asch, the obedience demonstrations of Stanley Milgram, the marshmallow self-control task associated with Walter Mischel — and the reader would accept that the result was settled. Few graduate students were rewarded for repeating an existing study with a fresh sample, and journals showed little appetite for publishing the kind of negative finding that would have followed from any rigorous attempt. By the early 2010s, however, a quiet unease about this arrangement had begun to crystallise into something more public. The Open Science Collaboration, a consortium of more than 270 researchers coordinated by Professor Brian Nosek at the University of Virginia, attempted to replicate 100 studies drawn from leading psychology journals and reported, in 2015, that fewer than forty per cent yielded a clearly significant result the second time round.

The reaction was sharp and divided. Some commentators, most prominently Professor Daniel Kahneman of Princeton, accepted the finding as evidence that a generation of work on social priming — the idea that subtle environmental cues exert measurable effects on subsequent behaviour — required substantial revision. Kahneman, whose own influential textbook had relied on several of the very studies in question, conceded in an open letter that the field had been "too credulous" and that the absence of multi-site replications had allowed weak effects to acquire an unwarranted permanence. Others rejected this framing more sharply. Professor Lisa Feldman Barrett, of Northeastern University, argued that a failed replication does not, on its own, establish that the original effect is illusory, since differences in sample composition, cultural context and procedural detail can suppress an effect that nevertheless operates under more favourable conditions.

The first sustained attempt to integrate these positions appeared around 2018, when a research team led by Dr Joseph Simmons at the University of Pennsylvania proposed that the crisis was less about isolated faulty studies and more about a structural feature of the discipline: the cumulative effect of small, individually defensible methodological choices that, taken together, inflate the apparent strength of findings. Simmons coined the term "researcher degrees of freedom" to describe the flexibility researchers enjoy in selecting which outcome measures to report, when to stop data collection and how to define a participant for exclusion. A subsequent multi-laboratory project, the Many Labs initiative, attempted to repeat thirteen well-known effects across thirty-six independent sites; some held up consistently, others varied dramatically with the sampled population, and a small number failed to appear at any site. The disaggregated picture, Simmons argued, undercut both the most pessimistic claim — that nothing in social psychology is real — and the most optimistic — that replication failures are largely artefacts of the replicators' incompetence.

Defenders of the original studies have, in turn, accepted some of these arguments while resisting others. They concede that pre-registration of hypotheses, larger samples and more transparent reporting would improve the literature, and that several individual findings should be retired. They argue, however, that the rhetorical conflation of "replication failure" with "fraud" or "wholesale invalidity" has caused real damage, including the unfair stigmatisation of researchers whose work simply explored more delicate effects. The distinction matters, in their view, because mid-career researchers, women and scholars from smaller institutions have absorbed a disproportionate share of the reputational cost. Critics have replied that this concern, while genuine, cannot be allowed to insulate the underlying methodological claims from scrutiny.

A separate and arguably more interesting strand of work has shifted the question from individual studies to the surrounding incentive structure. Researchers in metascience, including Dr Marcus Munafò of the University of Bristol, have argued that the more reliable lever for improving psychological research is not the disciplining of individual scientists but the redesign of journals, hiring committees and funding bodies. Munafò's group has documented that journals which mandate pre-registration and require the sharing of raw data report substantially higher replication rates for the studies they publish than those which do not. Such effects are difficult to capture in any single experiment, but appear with reasonable consistency in cross-journal comparisons. The implication, in his view, is that the durable improvement lies in the architecture of evaluation rather than in the conscience of any individual researcher.

Much hangs on how this is read. If the decade's central lesson is that publication incentives shape findings as powerfully as the data themselves, the reforms worth debating concern how doctoral training, peer review and promotion criteria are rebuilt, rather than which individual studies survive a given audit. A discipline that prizes only the original splash will, on this account, continue to produce the conditions that demand the next crisis. The argument demands a more rigorous appraisal than it has conventionally received, in the writer's view, partly because it is tougher to translate into a marketable product than a fresh dramatic finding.

To say all this is not to declare the methodological argument settled. Bayesian re-analyses conducted at the Centre for Open Science indicate that, once prior evidence is properly weighted, a number of contested findings retain diminished yet genuine support, especially where habitual rather than one-off behaviour is concerned. The replication crisis, on this reading, is neither the demolition some early commentators announced nor the minor housekeeping its critics allege. It is better understood as a slow renegotiation of what the discipline will accept as proof — a renegotiation that reaches into how careers are made, how journals operate, and how science answers to the public purse that sustains it.

audio_scripts.text: Good morning. Today's lecture extends our cognitive-science strand into the domain of long-term memory consolidation, drawing principally on the empirical literature from the past two decades. [pause:5s] The theoretical scaffolding I'll use comes from the work of Professor Aabid Choudhury — that's C-H-O-U-D-H-U-R-Y, with the silent D-H cluster pronounced like a soft Y. Choudhury's 2011 monograph reframed memory consolidation from a single overnight process into what he calls "iterative reconsolidation theory". [pause:3s] Firstly, a brief historical orientation. The seminal cohort study I'll reference today recruited participants in 2008 — sorry, I should correct that, 2006; the published results in 2008 reported on data collected in 2006. So whenever I refer to the recruitment year, please record 2006. [pause:3s] Right. Moving to terminology. The neurocognitive mechanism Choudhury highlights — a process in which previously consolidated memories return briefly to a labile state, are re-encoded, and then re-stabilised — is termed "reconsolidation". Now, you'll encounter related labels in the older literature: memory updating, trace renewal, post-retrieval modification. All of these gesture toward overlapping phenomena, but they are NOT interchangeable with reconsolidation. The currently accepted scholarly term is reconsolidation — r-e-c-o-n-s-o-l-i-d-a-t-i-o-n. So when the older literature uses memory updating or trace renewal, just remember they describe a similar but distinct construct. [pause:3s] The next domain I want to discuss is what cognitive psychologists call the "forgetting curve continuum". When researchers describe how unrehearsed material decays from working memory into long-term storage, they sketch a graded continuum running from initial encoding loss through interference decay to retrieval-induced suppression. So, kinda informally, you'll see a student who, you know, learns a hundred vocabulary items on Monday and recalls forty by Friday — that's interference decay. Or someone who can't recall a colleague's name precisely because they recently recalled a similar-sounding one — that's retrieval-induced suppression. Now, these are illustrative cases, not the technical term itself. The umbrella term is the forgetting curve continuum. [pause:3s] Now, the empirical data — and I want you to pay close attention here because the proportions cluster densely. Of the four hundred and twenty adult participants we tested across three laboratories last winter, MOST showed measurable consolidation benefit after a single night's sleep — roughly eighty-one per cent. Only a few — about seven per cent — exhibited no detectable consolidation effect, and some — twelve per cent — showed only marginal gains. So sleep-consolidation effects dominate numerically, but the seven-per-cent non-responder subset, though small, is theoretically significant for personalised cognitive therapy. [pause:3s] A second key construct I want to flag is "schema-driven distortion". This is the phenomenon whereby pre-existing mental frameworks systematically reshape what we recall, sometimes within minutes of encoding. At Marsden Cognitive Laboratory, our team documented one hundred and twelve instances of schema-driven distortion in the witness-recall paradigm during last year's testing window. [pause:3s] Crucially, the assumption that sleep simply strengthens all memory traces uniformly is, frankly, not supported. Most of our participants did NOT exhibit equivalent consolidation across declarative and procedural memory subsystems. Quite the contrary — many displayed selective consolidation, with motor-skill traces dominating over semantic-fact traces. So the older "uniform consolidation" hypothesis is empirically NOT corroborated by our data. [pause:3s] Let me return to a tense-orientation point worth flagging now. Choudhury's protocol USED TO require overnight in-lab polysomnography, NOW the field deploys wearable EEG headbands enabling home testing, and from 2028 a multi-centre consortium WILL be rolling out smartphone-based cognitive sampling. So past, present, future. For today's seminar, I want you to focus on the wearable-EEG methodology specifically — that is, the CURRENT protocol — not the legacy in-lab approach or the smartphone futures. So, sorta gonna concentrate on the present generation of headbands. [pause:3s] To summarise: memory consolidation is iterative not one-shot; the technical term for re-encoding of previously consolidated memories is reconsolidation; sleep-consolidation benefits dominate at roughly eighty-one per cent; and uniform consolidation is not empirically supported. Next week we'll examine attentional bottlenecks. Thank you. [pause:3s] (Q1) (Q2) (Q3) (Q4) (Q5) (Q6)

blocks.text: The two maps illustrate how the layout of mental health facilities in a British district was transformed between 1960 and 2020.

Overall, the most significant change is the dismantling of the single Central Psychiatric Hospital and its replacement by a network of four smaller, community-based care facilities — a layout consistent with the wider policy of deinstitutionalisation. Only the chapel and the residential street remained intact across the period.

In 1960, the Central Psychiatric Hospital dominated the site, occupying roughly two-thirds of the district, with the chapel to its north and open fields to its south. By 2020, this imposing structure had been entirely demolished. In its place, four specialised units were erected: a Community Mental Health Clinic in the north-central area, a Counselling Centre to the south-central, and a Crisis Care Unit adjacent to the eastern railway.

The southern fields, meanwhile, have been converted into a Rehabilitation Garden, while the western residential street is unchanged. The chapel, the only original structure left untouched, continues to occupy its position to the north.
The two maps depict the wholesale redevelopment of psychiatric provision in a British district across a sixty-year interval, contrasting its layout in 1960 with that of 2020.

Overall, what is most striking is the transition from a single, monolithic asylum to a dispersed constellation of specialised community facilities — a spatial expression of the deinstitutionalisation that reshaped mental-health policy. Barely two features survived the redevelopment untouched.

In the original layout, the Central Psychiatric Hospital dominated the district, sprawling across roughly two-thirds of the area; it was flanked by a modest chapel to the north and bordered by open fields to the south, with a railway tracing the eastern edge. By 2020, however, this imposing edifice had been razed in its entirety.

In its stead arose four discrete units: a Community Mental Health Clinic occupied the north-central plot, a Counselling Centre the south-central, and a Crisis Care Unit was sited adjacent to the railway. The southern fields, meanwhile, had given way to a Rehabilitation Garden. Only the chapel and the western residential street, left wholly unaltered, anchor the two maps to a common past.

idea_sections.heading: 10. Future trends / predictions — Xu hướng tương lai

blocks.text: Whereas earlier generations rarely discussed trauma openly, contemporary society increasingly treats psychological injury with the same seriousness as physical illness.
Unlike a fixed orthodoxy that dominated psychology decades ago, current research treats the brain as a dynamic organ shaped continuously by experience.
Compared with pure altruism, which is motivated by genuine concern for others, much prosocial behaviour today is driven by subtler social incentives.
Older approaches to mental illness relied heavily on institutionalisation, whereas modern practice favours community-based, cognitive-behavioural therapy-style intervention.
Twin studies comparing siblings raised apart offer compelling evidence for a genetic predisposition underlying certain personality traits.

idea_sections.heading: 12. Examples / evidence types — Loại ví dụ / minh chứng

blocks.text: The sharp increase in mental-health problems among young people over recent decades is one of the most concerning public-health trends of our era. This essay will examine the principal causes of this rise and propose practical measures that governments and societies might adopt.

Several interrelated factors appear to be driving this crisis. First and foremost, the omnipresence of social media has reshaped adolescent psychology. The constant exposure to idealised lives online seems to fuel chronic comparison and low self-esteem, and it is precisely this comparison culture that researchers link to rising rates of depression and anxiety. Secondly, today's hyper-competitive academic environment, combined with growing job insecurity and an unaffordable housing market, places young people under sustained psychological pressure. Finally, the gradual erosion of close family ties and community networks has left many adolescents feeling isolated, which exacerbates their underlying vulnerability.

A multi-pronged response is therefore needed. The most immediate measure is to integrate mental-health education into the school curriculum, so that students learn emotional regulation, resilience and introspection alongside their academic subjects. Governments could also subsidise cognitive-behavioural therapy for young patients, since the cost of private counselling remains prohibitive for many families. Furthermore, regulating social-media platforms — for example, by introducing age-gating and reducing algorithmic exposure to harmful content — might reduce some of the psychological pressures the technology imposes.

In conclusion, the deteriorating mental health of young people stems from a convergence of digital, economic and social pressures. Tackling it will require coordinated action across schools, healthcare and technology policy, since no single intervention can address all the dimensions of this complex problem.

The precipitous deterioration in youth mental health over the past two decades has emerged as one of the defining public-health challenges of our time. Disentangling its causes is essential if remedial measures are to be properly targeted; otherwise, interventions risk treating symptoms rather than aetiologies.

Several converging strands appear to underlie the crisis. Foremost among them is the saturation of adolescent life by algorithmically curated social media, which fosters incessant upward comparison and, by extension, narcissistic injury. Longitudinal data document a step-change in adolescent depressive symptomatology from roughly 2012 onward, coinciding tellingly with mass smartphone adoption. Compounding this is the hyper-competitive schooling environment and an increasingly precarious labour market, both of which generate sustained allostatic load. Were community and familial scaffolding still intact, such pressures might be cushioned; yet the documented hollowing-out of in-person networks, now framed as a loneliness epidemic, has stripped many young people of precisely those protective buffers.

Addressing this constellation of risk factors will require a multi-layered strategy. First, schools should embed psychoeducation — covering emotional regulation, cognitive restructuring and metacognitive awareness — into the core curriculum from an early age, drawing on evidence-based models such as Finland's KiVa programme. Second, public systems must subsidise cognitive-behavioural therapy, given that out-of-pocket costs remain prohibitive for most families, while parallel campaigns destigmatise help-seeking. Third, regulators ought to impose meaningful constraints on platform design, including default screen-time limits and algorithmic transparency obligations; Australia's 2024 under-16 legislation, contentious as it is, offers a precedent worth scrutinising.

In sum, the youth mental-health crisis is not reducible to any single cause, and neither, accordingly, is its solution. Only through coordinated action spanning educational, clinical and regulatory domains can the trajectory plausibly be reversed; piecemeal measures, however well-intentioned, will founder on the problem's sheer complexity.

solutions.text: Phần A — Viết lại câu

1. Some people demonstrate remarkable resilience in the face of hardship, bouncing back far faster than others. — "Resilience" là danh từ trừu tượng không đếm được, thường đi với "remarkable/psychological resilience" hoặc "resilience in the face of adversity".

2. A good counsellor needs a high degree of empathy in order to understand what a client is feeling from the inside. — "Empathy" (đặt mình vào cảm xúc người khác), khác với "sympathy" (thương cảm); thường đi với "show/cultivate empathy towards sb".

3. Many patients say that finally talking about a painful memory is a cathartic experience, bringing an enormous emotional release. — "Cathartic" là tính từ, hay đi với "a cathartic experience/moment"; chú ý "th" phát âm /θ/, không phải /k/.

4. Scientists now agree that a child's brain remains malleable well into adulthood, capable of being shaped and changed. — "Malleable" (dễ uốn nắn về tư duy/tính cách), thường dùng với "remain malleable" hoặc "a malleable mind".

5. Some of our habits are governed by subconscious processes that we are not even aware of. — "Subconscious" (tiềm thức, vẫn ảnh hưởng hành vi dù ta không ý thức được), khác với "unconscious" (bất tỉnh); hay đi với "subconscious biases/the subconscious mind".

6. Volunteers who give up their weekends to help strangers without expecting anything in return demonstrate genuine altruism. — "Altruism" là danh từ trừu tượng chỉ lòng vị tha; không dùng để miêu tả trực tiếp một người, nên đi với "an act of altruism" hoặc "genuine/pure altruism".
7. Constantly posting edited photos for admiration can be a sign of narcissism. — "Narcissism" là danh từ (chứng ái kỷ); tính từ tương ứng là "narcissistic", không phải "narcissism behaviour".

8. Keeping a journal for quiet introspection can reveal thought patterns you never noticed. — "Introspection" (tự xét nội tâm), khác với "inspection" (kiểm tra bên ngoài); hay đi với "a period of introspection" hoặc "practise introspection".

9. Because both of her parents suffered from anxiety, she may have a genetic predisposition to developing it too. — Cấu trúc chuẩn là "a predisposition to/towards sth", không dùng "for"; đây là khuynh hướng bẩm sinh, thường do di truyền.

10. Losing a parent at a young age can leave a lasting psychological trauma that lingers for decades. — "Trauma" (sang chấn tâm lý), khác với "stress" (căng thẳng nhẹ, tạm thời); hay đi với "childhood/psychological trauma" hoặc "process/overcome trauma".

11. The doctor explained that her chronic headaches were entirely psychosomatic, with no physical cause to be found. — "Psychosomatic" (triệu chứng thể chất bắt nguồn từ tâm lý); chữ "p" đầu là âm câm, trọng âm rơi vào "MAT".

12. Researchers are still grappling with why some people recover from depression faster than others. — "Grapple with" luôn đi kèm giới từ "with" (vật lộn để giải quyết một vấn đề khó), không dùng "grapple sth".
Phần B — Nâng cấp câu

1. Band 7: Chronic stress can trigger psychosomatic symptoms even when there is no underlying physical illness. Band 8: What often goes unnoticed is that the body can manifest psychological strain as genuine physical symptoms — a phenomenon clinicians term psychosomatic illness. (cleft + nominalisation)

2. Band 7: Children who receive consistent parental affection tend to grow up with greater self-confidence and emotional security. Band 8: It is, in large part, the quality of early parental bonds — as attachment theory suggests — that shapes a child's confidence well into adulthood. (cleft + reduced relative)

3. Band 7: People often fall prey to confirmation bias, favouring information that supports their existing beliefs. Band 8: Rarely do we seek out evidence that contradicts our convictions; instead, confirmation bias quietly steers us towards whatever confirms what we already believe. (negative inversion)

4. Band 7: Regular physical exercise can significantly alleviate symptoms of anxiety and low mood. Band 8: Were exercise prescribed as readily as medication, the burden of anxiety and depressive symptoms would, in all likelihood, be considerably lighter. (conditional inversion + hedging)

5. Band 7: A difficult childhood can have a lasting psychological impact that persists well into adulthood. Band 8: Traumatic as a difficult childhood may be, its effects, in most cases, can be mitigated through sustained therapeutic intervention and a supportive environment. (concession inversion + hedging)

6. Band 7: Governments should allocate significantly more resources to mental health services and early intervention. Band 8: Not only would greater investment in mental health services ease individual suffering, but it would also, on virtually any reading of the evidence, yield substantial economic returns. (negative inversion + hedging)

7. Band 7: Therapy can help individuals gain insight into the underlying causes of their behaviour. Band 8: It is through sustained introspection, guided by a trained therapist, that individuals typically come to understand the root causes of their own behaviour. (cleft + reduced relative)

8. Band 7: Excessive exposure to social media can exacerbate young people's tendency to compare themselves unfavourably with others. Band 8: What social media exacerbates, more than anything else, is a corrosive culture of comparison — one that leaves many young people questioning their own self-worth. (cleft + nominalisation)

blocks.text: 1. Facts & Trends (Dữ liệu thực tế để support cho bài Writing)

The EQ Revolution: Modern corporate recruiters often prioritise Emotional Intelligence (EQ) over IQ, noting that empathy and stress management are better predictors of leadership success than pure intellect.
Social Media and the Psyche: The constant exposure to idealised lives online is exacerbating neurotic behaviours and narcissism among teens, leading to a spike in youth depression.
Destigmatizing Mental Health: Seeking therapy is becoming normalised in modern society; it is increasingly viewed as maintaining "mental hygiene" rather than a sign of weakness.
2. Main Ideas Bank (Arguments)
Topic: EQ vs. IQ (Which is more important for success?)
Arguments for IQ: Essential for highly technical or academic fields (medicine, engineering, physics); determines the absolute limit of cognitive processing and problem-solving speed.

Arguments for EQ: Crucial for teamwork, networking, and leadership; helps individuals navigate workplace politics and maintain a positive mindset under pressure; prevents burnout through healthy coping mechanisms.
Topic: Nature vs. Nurture (Genetics vs. Environment in shaping personality)
Nature (Genetics): Studies on separated twins show striking similarities in temperament and intuition, proving a strong biological baseline for personality.
Nurture (Environment): The brain is highly malleable in formative years; social conditioning, childhood trauma, and education can completely override genetic predispositions.
Topic: The Mental Health Crisis (Causes & Solutions)
Causes: The fast-paced, hyper-competitive nature of modern urban life; social isolation exacerbated by technology; job insecurity and financial pressures.

Solutions: Implementing mental health education in the school curriculum (teaching resilience and emotional regulation); subsidising psychological counseling; promoting a work-life balance to reduce chronic stress.

Cue Card
Describe a time when you overcame a mental obstacle.
You should say:
what the obstacle was
when and where it happened
how you overcame it
and explain how you felt afterwards.
Prep Notes
OBSTACLE: paralysing public-speaking anxiety, university year 2
WHEN/WHERE: thesis defence prep, faculty hall
HOW: cognitive reframing, gradual exposure, breathwork
AFTER: liberated, transformed mindset, lasting impact
Model Answer (270 words)

The mental obstacle that most decisively shaped me was a debilitating bout of public-speaking anxiety I battled during my second year at university — a phase neurobiologists would describe as the prefrontal hijack of acute social-evaluative threat. (reduced relative)

It was during the run-up to my thesis defence — held in the cavernous main hall of the faculty — that the symptoms peaked: insomnia, psychosomatic chest tightness, and a creeping dread that bordered on panic. (cleft) For weeks, as if held hostage by my own amygdala, I genuinely contemplated dropping out.

What ultimately broke the cycle was a deliberate, multi-pronged intervention. (cleft) First, I began introspective journaling to externalise the rumination. Second, I sought out a campus counsellor who introduced me to cognitive behavioural reframing — the practice of identifying catastrophic thoughts and substituting evidence-based alternatives. Third, I practised graduated exposure, presenting to two friends, then five, then a study group of twenty.

Were I to identify the turning point, it would be the moment I internalised that the brain is genuinely malleable — a notion underpinned by neuroplasticity research. (conditional inversion) Not only did the symptoms recede, but I also began to look forward to public speaking. (negative inversion)

The aftermath felt nothing short of liberating. The acquisition of these coping strategies has, in all likelihood, paid dividends in every subsequent presentation, interview, and even social interaction. (nominalisation + hedging)

To borrow an idiom, I had been on the verge of cracking up (informal idiom), but I came out the other side with my head firmly screwed on (informal idiom) — and a far more growth-oriented mindset than I'd ever thought possible.
Examiner Follow-up
"Do you think mental obstacles can ever truly be overcome, or do they always come back?"

Suggested response (42 words): Honestly, what I've come to accept is that they're rarely eliminated outright — they recede, then occasionally resurface. Were one to expect a permanent cure, disappointment would be inevitable. Building resilience, however, transforms the relationship with the obstacle itself.

blocks.text: Q1. Why has mental illness increased in modern society?

P: The surge in mental illness is, in my view, a multi-causal phenomenon rather than the product of any single factor — a confluence of digital saturation, socio-economic precarity, and shifting social fabric.
E: Chronic stressors erode resilience, while atomised lifestyles deny individuals the buffering protection that close-knit communities once provided.

E: WHO's 2022 World Mental Health Report revealed that depression and anxiety prevalence surged by 25% in the first year of the pandemic alone, with 970 million people worldwide now living with a mental disorder. The Lancet Commission on Adolescent Mental Health (2023) linked heavy social-media use (>3 hrs/day) to a 60% higher risk of depressive symptoms. OECD (2021) data further shows that workplace stress costs member economies an estimated 4% of GDP annually.
L: Hence, what we're witnessing isn't fragility but rather the predictable psychological cost of a hyper-competitive, screen-mediated, socially atomised modernity.
Hedging Toolbox: the data consistently suggest / it is widely acknowledged that / for the most part
Lexical Upgrade Box:
more problems → rising prevalence / surging incidence
stress → chronic psychological strain
sad → depressive symptoms / clinical depression
Sample Answer (96 words):

The data consistently suggest mental illness has risen due to overlapping pressures. WHO (2022) documented a 25% spike in depression and anxiety post-pandemic, with 970 million globally affected. The Lancet Commission (2023) linked heavy social-media use to a 60% higher risk of depressive symptoms. What's often overlooked is the erosion of community: OECD (2021) ties workplace stress to 4% of GDP in lost productivity. Were modern life less atomised and less algorithmically curated for outrage, prevalence would, in all likelihood, fall. It's not that we're weaker — it's that the stressors are unprecedented.
Q2. Is therapy more effective than medication?
P: Therapy and medication are, strictly speaking, not competitors but complements — though their relative effectiveness varies considerably by diagnosis and severity.
E: Talk therapy excels at addressing the root cognitive distortions and behavioural patterns, while pharmacotherapy can rapidly stabilise neurochemistry in acute presentations.

E: A landmark meta-analysis published in The Lancet Psychiatry (Cuijpers et al., 2020) examining 101 trials concluded that combined therapy plus medication outperformed either alone for moderate-to-severe depression, with effect sizes around 0.4–0.6. NICE guidelines (UK, updated 2022) recommend CBT as first-line for mild depression and combined treatment for severe cases. The WHO Mental Health Action Plan 2013–2030 further emphasises evidence-based integrated care.
L: Therefore, framing this as therapy versus medication is, frankly, a false dichotomy — best practice integrates both, tailored to clinical need.
Hedging Toolbox: the clinical evidence broadly supports / it would be misleading to suggest / depending on context
Lexical Upgrade Box:
talking → psychotherapy / talk-based interventions
pills → pharmacotherapy / psychotropic medication
better → more efficacious / clinically superior
Sample Answer (94 words):

It would be misleading to suggest therapy is universally better than medication. The Lancet Psychiatry meta-analysis (Cuijpers, 2020) found that combined treatment outperforms either modality alone for moderate-to-severe depression, with effect sizes of 0.4–0.6. NICE guidelines (2022) likewise recommend CBT as first-line for mild cases but combined care for severe presentations. Were one to dismiss medication as a crutch, one would ignore decades of pharmacological evidence; conversely, treating with pills alone neglects the cognitive restructuring therapy provides. By and large, the dichotomy is false — the answer is "both, judiciously".
Q3. Should mental health be a national priority?
P: Mental health must be elevated to the status of a national priority, on a par with physical health — both on moral grounds and as a matter of hard economic calculation.

E: Untreated mental illness imposes staggering economic costs through lost productivity, healthcare expenditure, and premature mortality, while early intervention yields among the highest returns of any public-health investment.

E: WHO (2022) estimates depression and anxiety alone cost the global economy $1 trillion annually in lost productivity, yet every $1 invested in scaled-up treatment yields a $4 return in improved health and productivity. OECD (2021) likewise found mental ill-health costs member states roughly 4.2% of GDP. Despite this, WHO (2022) notes governments spend, on average, only 2% of health budgets on mental health — a figure described as "wholly inadequate".
L: Consequently, treating mental health as discretionary spending is not merely ethically indefensible but economically irrational.
Hedging Toolbox: the case is, in my view, compelling / it can scarcely be denied that / on virtually any reading of the data
Lexical Upgrade Box:
important → a strategic priority / a national imperative
spend money → *allocate resources / invest in
help people → deliver evidence-based interventions
Sample Answer (96 words):

On virtually any reading of the data, mental health should be a national priority. WHO (2022) estimates depression and anxiety cost the global economy $1 trillion annually, yet every $1 invested in scaled-up treatment returns $4 — among the highest ROIs in public health. OECD (2021) puts the total cost at 4.2% of GDP. Despite this, governments spend just 2% of health budgets on mental health on average. Were policymakers to act on the evidence, they'd shift resources accordingly. Not only is the case morally compelling, but it's also fiscally indefensible to continue under-investing.
T06 — PSYCHOLOGY & THE HUMAN MIND (Advanced C1, Band 7.5–8.0)
1. Section Type + Lecturer Info
Section: IELTS Listening Section 4 — academic monologue, no Q&A
Lecturer: Dr. Marcus Lindqvist, clinical neuropsychologist
Academic field: Cognitive Neuroscience / Clinical Psychology
Topic of lecture: "Neuroplasticity, Psychosomatic Symptoms and Cognitive Bias: How a Malleable Brain Rewrites Attachment"
2. Pre-listening Vocab Brush-up (Band 7+)
neuroplasticity (n) — the brain's capacity to reorganise its neural pathways
psychosomatic (adj) — physical symptoms caused or worsened by mental factors
cognitive bias (n phrase) — systematic deviation from rational judgement
attachment theory (n phrase) — Bowlby's framework on early bonding and adult relationships
malleable (adj) — capable of being shaped or moulded; pliable
3. Predict 3 Ideas (Advanced)
The lecturer will likely explain that neuroplasticity allows trauma survivors to "rewire" maladaptive cognitive patterns.
He may discuss psychosomatic symptoms as evidence of mind-body interconnection.
A discussion of attachment theory will probably link childhood bonding to adult cognitive biases.
4. Transcript (≈600 words)

Good afternoon, everyone. Today's lecture brings together three threads from earlier weeks — neuroplasticity, psychosomatic illness and cognitive bias — and weaves them, um, into the contemporary discussion of attachment theory. [pause]

Let's begin with a striking finding. For most of the twentieth century, neuroscientists assumed the adult brain was, well, more or less fixed by the age of twenty-five. Recent imaging studies, however, have utterly demolished that orthodoxy. The brain remains remarkably malleable throughout life — a phenomenon now universally termed neuroplasticity. The clinical implication is profound: maladaptive patterns laid down by early trauma can, in principle, be rewired through sustained therapeutic intervention. [pause]

This brings me neatly to psychosomatic symptoms. Patients frequently present with chronic stomach pain, migraines, even, indeed, partial paralysis — for which no organic cause can be found. Critically, these are not imagined; the suffering is genuine. Rather, the subconscious is, in effect, externalising distress that the conscious mind has failed to process. Verbalising the underlying memory — sometimes called the cathartic moment — often produces remarkable, measurable relief. [pause]

Now, where do cognitive biases fit in? Well, attachment theory — first formulated by Bowlby in the 1950s — holds that the quality of our earliest bonds becomes a template for adult relationships. Insecure attachment, for example, breeds what psychologists term confirmation bias in social settings: we unconsciously seek evidence that others will, eventually, disappoint us. [pause]

Right, before we wrap up, I want to add a layer of caution, because there's a tendency — especially in popular psychology — to treat neuroplasticity as an unqualified gift, an inner reset button. It isn't, quite. Let me point you to the work of Norman Doidge and, more rigorously, the longitudinal imaging done at the Max Planck Institute. Plasticity, it turns out, is fundamentally agnostic — it entrenches the maladaptive just as readily as the adaptive. Chronic rumination, for instance, doesn't merely reflect a depressed state; it physically deepens the neural grooves that sustain it. So the very mechanism we hope to harness in therapy is, um, the same mechanism that manufactured the pathology in the first place. The brain, if you like, has no opinion about your wellbeing. [pause]

This connects rather neatly to a fascinating study on attachment I'd flag — Sroufe and Egeland's Minnesota cohort, which followed children from birth into their thirties. What they demonstrated is that an insecure early template is not destiny. A substantial subset of their participants — they coined the lovely term "earned secure" — had endured frankly dreadful childhoods, yet through a single corrective relationship, often with a therapist or a partner, they reorganised that internal working model entirely. So the confirmation bias I mentioned, the unconscious hunt for disappointment, can be overwritten. Not erased — overwritten. [pause]

A further consideration, and this complicates the cathartic-relief story, is that mere verbalisation can sometimes re-traumatise rather than release. Catharsis without regulation, without a sense of safety in the room, can simply re-fire the distress circuitry. Timing and containment, in other words, matter enormously. [pause]

So plasticity, attachment and somatic insight together hand clinicians a genuinely powerful but double-edged toolkit. And that double edge, I think, is exactly where the question of access and resourcing becomes acute — let me flag the key policy implication…

So, the therapeutic upshot, then, is this: by combining cognitive-behavioural reframing with somatic awareness, clinicians can leverage neuroplasticity to disrupt long-entrenched patterns. Before we close, do note that resilience — the capacity to recover from adversity — is itself trainable, not merely innate.

The two maps illustrate how the layout of mental health facilities in a British district was transformed between 1960 and 2020.

Overall, the most significant change is the dismantling of the single Central Psychiatric Hospital and its replacement by a network of four smaller, community-based care facilities — a layout consistent with the wider policy of deinstitutionalisation. Only the chapel and the residential street remained intact across the period.

In 1960, the Central Psychiatric Hospital dominated the site, occupying roughly two-thirds of the district, with the chapel to its north and open fields to its south. By 2020, this imposing structure had been entirely demolished. In its place, four specialised units were erected: a Community Mental Health Clinic in the north-central area, a Counselling Centre to the south-central, and a Crisis Care Unit adjacent to the eastern railway.

The southern fields, meanwhile, have been converted into a Rehabilitation Garden, while the western residential street is unchanged. The chapel, the only original structure left untouched, continues to occupy its position to the north.
(f) Bài mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~183 từ)
The two maps depict the wholesale redevelopment of psychiatric provision in a British district across a sixty-year interval, contrasting its layout in 1960 with that of 2020.

Overall, what is most striking is the transition from a single, monolithic asylum to a dispersed constellation of specialised community facilities — a spatial expression of the deinstitutionalisation that reshaped mental-health policy. Barely two features survived the redevelopment untouched.

In the original layout, the Central Psychiatric Hospital dominated the district, sprawling across roughly two-thirds of the area; it was flanked by a modest chapel to the north and bordered by open fields to the south, with a railway tracing the eastern edge. By 2020, however, this imposing edifice had been razed in its entirety.

In its stead arose four discrete units: a Community Mental Health Clinic occupied the north-central plot, a Counselling Centre the south-central, and a Crisis Care Unit was sited adjacent to the railway. The southern fields, meanwhile, had given way to a Rehabilitation Garden. Only the chapel and the western residential street, left wholly unaltered, anchor the two maps to a common past.
(g) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  B8 paraphrase tiêu đề mạnh hơn ('the wholesale redevelopment ... across a sixty-year interval') và overview dùng ẩn dụ không gian ('a spatial expression of deinstitutionalisation'), sâu hơn B7.
•  B8 đa dạng hoá cụm vị trí ('flanked by', 'bordered by', 'sited adjacent to', 'tracing the eastern edge') và động từ học thuật ('razed', 'arose', 'anchor'), trong khi B7 lặp 'to the X of'.
•  B8 chèn đảo ngữ/fronting ('In its stead arose four discrete units') và cấu trúc bị động hoàn thành ('had been razed in its entirety'), nâng GRA rõ so với B7.
(h) Chiến lược làm bài (5 bước)
•  Identify the focal change: the single asylum gives way to four smaller facilities (deinstitutionalisation).
•  List what remained unchanged — chapel and residential street — and group them into one stability sentence.
•  List what was demolished or replaced: the central hospital and the southern fields.
•  List what was added: four specialised units plus the Rehabilitation Garden, locating each with a cardinal direction.

blocks.text: (3) Ý tưởng hai chiều (Brainstorm)
Main causes:
•  Algorithmically curated social media fuels upward comparison; adolescent depression rose sharply from 2012, coinciding with smartphone saturation.
•  Hyper-competitive schooling, job-market precarity and unaffordable housing generate chronic, sustained stress.
•  Erosion of in-person community and family support has made loneliness a public-health emergency.
Measures:
•  School-based mental-health curricula teaching resilience, emotional regulation and introspection (e.g. Finland's KiVa programme).
•  Public subsidisation of cognitive-behavioural therapy plus campaigns to destigmatise help-seeking.
•  Regulation of social-media platforms — age-gating, algorithmic transparency, default screen-time limits (Australia's 2024 under-16 ban).

•  Body 2 — propose targeted measures: school psychoeducation, subsidised therapy, and platform regulation.

blocks.text: (7) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 7.0 (~264 words)

The sharp increase in mental-health problems among young people over recent decades is one of the most concerning public-health trends of our era. This essay will examine the principal causes of this rise and propose practical measures that governments and societies might adopt.

Several interrelated factors appear to be driving this crisis. First and foremost, the omnipresence of social media has reshaped adolescent psychology. The constant exposure to idealised lives online seems to fuel chronic comparison and low self-esteem, and it is precisely this comparison culture that researchers link to rising rates of depression and anxiety. Secondly, today's hyper-competitive academic environment, combined with growing job insecurity and an unaffordable housing market, places young people under sustained psychological pressure. Finally, the gradual erosion of close family ties and community networks has left many adolescents feeling isolated, which exacerbates their underlying vulnerability.

A multi-pronged response is therefore needed. The most immediate measure is to integrate mental-health education into the school curriculum, so that students learn emotional regulation, resilience and introspection alongside their academic subjects. Governments could also subsidise cognitive-behavioural therapy for young patients, since the cost of private counselling remains prohibitive for many families. Furthermore, regulating social-media platforms — for example, by introducing age-gating and reducing algorithmic exposure to harmful content — might reduce some of the psychological pressures the technology imposes.

In conclusion, the deteriorating mental health of young people stems from a convergence of digital, economic and social pressures. Tackling it will require coordinated action across schools, healthcare and technology policy, since no single intervention can address all the dimensions of this complex problem.
(8) Bài luận mẫu — BAND 8.0 (~292 words)

The precipitous deterioration in youth mental health over the past two decades has emerged as one of the defining public-health challenges of our time. Disentangling its causes is essential if remedial measures are to be properly targeted; otherwise, interventions risk treating symptoms rather than aetiologies.

Several converging strands appear to underlie the crisis. Foremost among them is the saturation of adolescent life by algorithmically curated social media, which fosters incessant upward comparison and, by extension, narcissistic injury. Longitudinal data document a step-change in adolescent depressive symptomatology from roughly 2012 onward, coinciding tellingly with mass smartphone adoption. Compounding this is the hyper-competitive schooling environment and an increasingly precarious labour market, both of which generate sustained allostatic load. Were community and familial scaffolding still intact, such pressures might be cushioned; yet the documented hollowing-out of in-person networks, now framed as a loneliness epidemic, has stripped many young people of precisely those protective buffers.

Addressing this constellation of risk factors will require a multi-layered strategy. First, schools should embed psychoeducation — covering emotional regulation, cognitive restructuring and metacognitive awareness — into the core curriculum from an early age, drawing on evidence-based models such as Finland's KiVa programme. Second, public systems must subsidise cognitive-behavioural therapy, given that out-of-pocket costs remain prohibitive for most families, while parallel campaigns destigmatise help-seeking. Third, regulators ought to impose meaningful constraints on platform design, including default screen-time limits and algorithmic transparency obligations; Australia's 2024 under-16 legislation, contentious as it is, offers a precedent worth scrutinising.

In sum, the youth mental-health crisis is not reducible to any single cause, and neither, accordingly, is its solution. Only through coordinated action spanning educational, clinical and regulatory domains can the trajectory plausibly be reversed; piecemeal measures, however well-intentioned, will founder on the problem's sheer complexity.
(9) Phân tích nâng band 7 → 8
•  B8 mở bài bằng lexis cao cấp ('precipitous deterioration', 'aetiologies') và khung tư duy phân tích ('treating symptoms rather than aetiologies'), thay vì câu mở phẳng của B7.
•  B8 dùng số liệu định danh ('a step-change ... from roughly 2012', 'allostatic load', KiVa, luật Úc 2024) và register lâm sàng xuyên suốt, trong khi B7 giữ ví dụ chung chung.

•  B8 dày cấu trúc: fronting cleft ('Foremost among them is'), đảo ngữ điều kiện ('Were ... still intact'), đảo ngữ phủ định ('Only through ... can the trajectory ... be reversed'); B7 chủ yếu một cleft.

vocabulary.definition_en: a deeply distressing or disturbing experience that has a lasting psychological impact
vocabulary.definition_vi: sang chấn tâm lý, tổn thương tâm lý sâu sắc
vocabulary.example: Maladaptive patterns laid down by early trauma can, in principle, be rewired through sustained therapeutic intervention.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'trauma' (gốc Hy Lạp: vết thương) → vết thương tâm lý để lại hậu quả lâu dài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuộc về tâm sinh — triệu chứng thể chất bắt nguồn hoặc trầm trọng hơn do yếu tố tâm lý.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The doctor concluded that her recurring stomach pains were entirely **psychosomatic**, with no organic cause to be found.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'psycho-' (tâm trí) + 'somatic' (thuộc cơ thể) → bệnh của tâm trí biểu hiện ra cơ thể.
vocabulary.common_error: Chữ 'p' đầu từ 'psychosomatic' là âm câm, không phát âm /p/; trọng âm rơi vào âm tiết 'MAT'.
vocabulary.definition_en: (of physical symptoms or illness) caused or made worse by mental factors such as stress, rather than a purely physical cause
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuộc về tâm sinh (bệnh có nguồn gốc tâm lý, biểu hiện ra thể chất)
vocabulary.example: The doctor concluded that her recurring stomach pains were entirely psychosomatic, with no organic cause to be found.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'psycho-' (tâm trí) + 'somatic' (thuộc cơ thể) → bệnh của tâm trí biểu hiện ra cơ thể.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Tính khả biến thần kinh — khả năng của não bộ tự tổ chức lại các đường dẫn thần kinh suốt đời.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> It is **neuroplasticity** — the brain's lifelong capacity to rewire itself — that underwrites our ability to recover from psychological injury.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'neuro-' (thần kinh) + 'plasticity' (tính dẻo, dễ uốn như nhựa) → não bộ có thể tự "uốn nắn" lại.
vocabulary.common_error: Từ có 6 âm tiết, trọng âm chính rơi vào 'TIS', trọng âm phụ ở 'NEU'; đừng rút gọn thành 'plasticity' khi cần chỉ rõ ngữ cảnh của não bộ.
vocabulary.definition_en: the brain's lifelong capacity to reorganise and rewire its neural pathways in response to experience
vocabulary.definition_vi: tính khả biến thần kinh, khả năng tự tái cấu trúc của não bộ
vocabulary.example: It is neuroplasticity — the brain's lifelong capacity to rewire itself — that underwrites our ability to recover from psychological injury.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'neuro-' (thần kinh) + 'plasticity' (tính dẻo, dễ uốn như nhựa) → não bộ có thể tự "uốn nắn" lại.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thuyết gắn bó — khung lý thuyết của Bowlby cho rằng chất lượng gắn kết thời thơ ấu định hình quan hệ khi trưởng thành.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Attachment theory** holds that the quality of our earliest bonds becomes a template for adult relationships.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'attach' (gắn kết) + 'theory' → lý thuyết giải thích cách con người "gắn bó" từ nhỏ định hình quan hệ sau này.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Attachment' trong tâm lý học chỉ sự gắn bó tình cảm, không phải nghĩa 'đính kèm' (file đính kèm) trong tiếng Anh thông thường.
vocabulary.definition_en: Bowlby's psychological framework proposing that the quality of a child's earliest bonds shapes patterns in adult relationships
vocabulary.definition_vi: thuyết gắn bó, khung lý thuyết về sự gắn kết thời thơ ấu ảnh hưởng đến quan hệ trưởng thành
vocabulary.example: Attachment theory holds that the quality of our earliest bonds becomes a template for adult relationships.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'attach' (gắn kết) + 'theory' → lý thuyết giải thích cách con người "gắn bó" từ nhỏ định hình quan hệ sau này.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Vật lộn, nỗ lực đối mặt và tìm cách giải quyết một vấn đề khó khăn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Experts **grapple with** the ethics of therapy versus medication, often at the expense of a clear, unified policy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'grapple' gợi hình ảnh vật lộn tay đôi → "vật lộn" với một vấn đề khó nhằn.
vocabulary.common_error: Luôn đi kèm giới từ 'with': 'grapple with sth', không dùng 'grapple sth' hay 'grapple on sth'.
vocabulary.definition_en: to try hard to deal with or understand a difficult problem or issue
vocabulary.definition_vi: vật lộn, cố gắng đối mặt và giải quyết (một vấn đề khó)
vocabulary.example: Experts grapple with the ethics of therapy versus medication, often at the expense of a clear, unified policy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'grapple' gợi hình ảnh vật lộn tay đôi → "vật lộn" với một vấn đề khó nhằn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Sự yên tâm, cảm giác thanh thản, không còn lo lắng trong đầu.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Installing a modern security system gave us complete **peace of mind**.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'peace' (bình yên) + 'of mind' (trong tâm trí) → tâm trí bình yên, không lo âu.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Peace of mind' không dùng số nhiều 'peaces'; là cụm từ cố định không thể tách rời.
vocabulary.definition_en: a state of being free from worry or anxiety; mental calm and reassurance
vocabulary.definition_vi: sự yên tâm, thanh thản trong tâm trí
vocabulary.example: Installing a modern security system gave us complete peace of mind.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'peace' (bình yên) + 'of mind' (trong tâm trí) → tâm trí bình yên, không lo âu.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Đãng trí, hay quên do mải suy nghĩ những chuyện khác.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> My grandfather is quite **absent-minded**; he often forgets where his glasses are.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'absent' (vắng mặt) + 'minded' (trong đầu) → tâm trí "vắng mặt" khỏi thực tại → đãng trí.
vocabulary.common_error: Viết có gạch nối 'absent-minded', không viết rời 'absent minded' khi dùng làm tính từ đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: so lost in thought or preoccupied that one forgets things or fails to notice what is happening
vocabulary.definition_vi: đãng trí, hay quên (do mải suy nghĩ chuyện khác)
vocabulary.example: My grandfather is quite absent-minded; he often forgets where his glasses are.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'absent' (vắng mặt) + 'minded' (trong đầu) → tâm trí "vắng mặt" khỏi thực tại → đãng trí.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Cởi mở, sẵn sàng đón nhận những ý tưởng và góc nhìn mới.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Travelling helps you become more **open-minded** and accept different perspectives.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'open' (mở) + 'minded' (trong đầu) → đầu óc "mở" ra để đón nhận điều mới.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm với 'open mind' (danh từ, 'a mind that is open') — 'open-minded' là tính từ ghép có gạch nối.
vocabulary.definition_en: willing to consider new ideas and different perspectives without prejudice
vocabulary.definition_vi: cởi mở, sẵn sàng tiếp nhận ý tưởng và quan điểm mới
vocabulary.example: Travelling helps you become more open-minded and accept different perspectives.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'open' (mở) + 'minded' (trong đầu) → đầu óc "mở" ra để đón nhận điều mới.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Kém thích nghi — hành vi hay lối tư duy đối phó nhưng gây hại về lâu dài.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> **Maladaptive** patterns laid down by early trauma can, in principle, be rewired through sustained therapeutic intervention.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'mal-' (xấu, tiền tố Latin) + 'adaptive' (thích nghi) → thích nghi theo cách xấu, gây hại về lâu dài.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'maladaptive' (kém thích nghi, gây hại) với 'maladjusted' (mất cân bằng tâm lý nói chung, ít mang tính học thuật hơn).
vocabulary.definition_en: (of behaviour or a coping pattern) not conducive to adaptation or good adjustment; harmful in the long run despite serving a short-term purpose
vocabulary.definition_vi: kém thích nghi, mang tính đối phó tiêu cực (về hành vi/lối tư duy)
vocabulary.example: Maladaptive patterns laid down by early trauma can, in principle, be rewired through sustained therapeutic intervention.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'mal-' (xấu, tiền tố Latin) + 'adaptive' (thích nghi) → thích nghi theo cách xấu, gây hại về lâu dài.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Thiên kiến xác nhận — xu hướng chỉ tìm và tin vào thông tin củng cố niềm tin có sẵn.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Insecure attachment breeds what psychologists term **confirmation bias** in social settings: we unconsciously seek evidence that others will eventually disappoint us.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'confirmation' (xác nhận) + 'bias' (thiên vị) → chỉ tin những gì "xác nhận" điều mình đã nghĩ sẵn.
vocabulary.common_error: Đây là một loại cụ thể của 'cognitive bias'; đừng dùng hai thuật ngữ thay thế lẫn nhau như thể chúng đồng nghĩa hoàn toàn.
vocabulary.definition_en: the tendency to search for, interpret, and recall information in a way that confirms one's pre-existing beliefs
vocabulary.definition_vi: thiên kiến xác nhận, xu hướng chỉ tin vào điều củng cố niềm tin sẵn có
vocabulary.example: Insecure attachment breeds what psychologists term confirmation bias in social settings: we unconsciously seek evidence that others will eventually disappoint us.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'confirmation' (xác nhận) + 'bias' (thiên vị) → chỉ tin những gì "xác nhận" điều mình đã nghĩ sẵn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Quan điểm chính thống — niềm tin đã được chấp nhận rộng rãi, nay có thể đang bị thách thức.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Recent imaging studies have utterly demolished that **orthodoxy**, revealing that the adult brain remains remarkably malleable.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'ortho-' (đúng, thẳng) + 'doxa' (ý kiến, gốc Hy Lạp) → "ý kiến đúng đắn" được số đông công nhận.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'orthodoxy' (quan điểm chính thống được chấp nhận rộng rãi) với 'orthodontics' (chỉnh nha, nha khoa).
vocabulary.definition_en: an established, widely accepted belief or theory, especially one now being challenged
vocabulary.definition_vi: quan điểm chính thống, niềm tin đã được chấp nhận rộng rãi (thường sắp bị lung lay)
vocabulary.example: Recent imaging studies have utterly demolished that orthodoxy, revealing that the adult brain remains remarkably malleable.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'ortho-' (đúng, thẳng) + 'doxa' (ý kiến, gốc Hy Lạp) → "ý kiến đúng đắn" được số đông công nhận.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Làm trầm trọng thêm, khiến một vấn đề hay cảm giác tiêu cực trở nên xấu đi.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> The erosion of community ties **exacerbates** adolescents' underlying vulnerability to mental-health problems.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
'exacerbate' nghe gần 'acid' (a-xít) → như đổ thêm a-xít vào vết thương → làm tệ hơn.
vocabulary.common_error: Đừng nhầm 'exacerbate' (làm trầm trọng thêm một vấn đề) với 'exasperate' (làm ai đó bực bội, tức giận).
vocabulary.definition_en: to make a problem, situation, or negative feeling worse
vocabulary.definition_vi: làm trầm trọng thêm, làm xấu đi (một vấn đề)
vocabulary.example: The erosion of community ties exacerbates adolescents' underlying vulnerability to mental-health problems.
vocabulary.memory_hook: 'exacerbate' nghe gần 'acid' (a-xít) → như đổ thêm a-xít vào vết thương → làm tệ hơn.

vocabulary.body_markdown:
Một giải pháp đa hướng, giải quyết vấn đề từ nhiều góc độ cùng lúc.

## Ví dụ IELTS Speaking Part 3
> Tackling the youth mental-health crisis demands **a multi-pronged response** across sectors, from schools to healthcare to technology policy.

## Ghi nhớ nhanh
Hình ảnh cái chĩa nhiều răng (prongs) đâm vào vấn đề từ nhiều hướng cùng lúc → giải pháp đa hướng.
vocabulary.common_error: 'Prong' vốn nghĩa 'răng của cái chĩa'; 'multi-pronged' luôn viết có gạch nối khi đứng trước danh từ.
vocabulary.definition_en: a solution or strategy that tackles a problem simultaneously from several different angles or methods
vocabulary.definition_vi: một giải pháp đa hướng, tiếp cận vấn đề từ nhiều phía cùng lúc
vocabulary.example: Tackling the youth mental-health crisis demands a multi-pronged response across sectors, from schools to healthcare to technology policy.
vocabulary.memory_hook: Hình ảnh cái chĩa nhiều răng (prongs) đâm vào vấn đề từ nhiều hướng cùng lúc → giải pháp đa hướng.
